```{python}
#| echo: false

import great_docs as gd

gd.enable_tbl_preview(n_head=8, n_tail=3)
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: false
import os
import tempfile

os.chdir(tempfile.mkdtemp())
```

Networks travel between programs as files. A protein interaction network arrives from a database
as a tab-separated edge list, a social network drawn in Gephi is saved as GEXF, a citation graph
comes from a collaborator as GraphML, and a figure for a paper needs TikZ code. EdgeCase reads and
writes all of these, and more, with a pair of top-level functions for each format: `from_*()`
reads a file into a new `Graph`, and `to_*()` writes a graph out.

The formats differ mostly in how much of a graph they can hold. Some keep every node and edge
attribute with its type, some keep only the structure, and the rest fall in between:

| Format | Read | Write | Keeps | Common sources and uses |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| GraphML | `from_graphml()` | `to_graphml()` | everything, with types | NetworkX, igraph, Gephi, Cytoscape, yEd |
| GEXF | `from_gexf()` | `to_gexf()` | everything, plus layout and colors | Gephi |
| GML | `from_gml()` | `to_gml()` | everything, booleans as 0 and 1 | network science data collections |
| Pajek | `from_pajek()` | `to_pajek()` | labels, weights, scalar attributes, coordinates | Pajek, older social network data |
| LEDA | `from_leda()` | `to_leda()` | labels and weights | the LEDA library, graph benchmarks |
| Edge list | `from_tsv_edge_list()` | `to_tsv_edge_list()` | edges and weights | BioGRID, STRING, spreadsheets |
| SIF | `from_sif()` | `to_sif()` | edges and their interaction types | Cytoscape |
| Matrix Market | `from_matrix_market()` | — | edges and weights | SuiteSparse, network repositories |
| Adjacency list | `from_adjlist()`, `from_multiline_adjlist()` | `to_adjlist()`, `to_multiline_adjlist()` | structure, or edges with data | NetworkX |
| Node-link JSON | `from_node_link()` | `to_node_link()` | everything | D3.js, NetworkX, web applications |
| Cytoscape.js JSON | `from_cytoscape()` | `to_cytoscape()` | everything, plus positions | Cytoscape.js, Cytoscape desktop |
| Adjacency JSON | `from_adjacency_data()` | `to_adjacency_data()` | everything | NetworkX |
| Tree JSON | `from_tree_data()` | `to_tree_data()` | trees, with node attributes | D3.js hierarchies |
| graph6, sparse6 | `from_graph6()`, `from_sparse6()` | `to_graph6()`, `to_sparse6()` | structure only | nauty, the House of Graphs |
| DOT | `from_dot()` | `to_dot()` | everything, as strings | Graphviz, build and compiler tools |
| TikZ | — | `to_latex()`, `to_latex_raw()` | a drawing | LaTeX documents |
| Cypher | `from_cypher()` | `to_cypher()` | labels, types, properties | Neo4j, Memgraph |

Each function takes a path as a string or a `pathlib.Path`. The text formats can also be read from
a string holding the data itself, and their writers return the text when no path is given. This
page goes through the formats in families, with an example of each, and ends with the general
route for tabular files such as CSV and Parquet.

## A graph to exchange

The examples on this page use a small network of four researchers, who have written papers together
and shared code, with a few attributes of different types on the nodes and the edges. `type` and
`rel` are EdgeCase's built-in node types and relationship types (see
[The graph model](03-graph-model.qmd)), and the weights count the joint papers:

```{python}
import edgecase as ec
import polars as pl
from pathlib import Path

lab = ec.Graph(weighted=True, graph_name="lab")
lab.add_node("Ada", type="faculty", since=2009, tenured=True)
lab.add_node("Bo", type="postdoc", since=2021, tenured=False)
lab.add_node("Cleo", type="student", since=2022, tenured=False)
lab.add_node("Dev", type="student", since=2023, tenured=False)
lab.add_edge("Ada", "Bo", weight=5.0, rel="coauthor")
lab.add_edge("Ada", "Cleo", weight=2.0, rel="coauthor")
lab.add_edge("Bo", "Cleo", weight=1.0, rel="code")
lab.get_node_df()
```

Dev has no collaborations yet, which makes the network a good test of whether a format keeps
isolated nodes. The edges:

```{python}
lab.get_edge_df()
```

## GraphML

GraphML is an XML format and the most widely supported way of exchanging graphs with attributes.
NetworkX, igraph, Gephi, Cytoscape, and yEd all read and write it, and many bioinformatics tools
export it. Each attribute is declared once, with a name and a type, and then given for each node or
edge that has it, so a file can be checked and read without guessing.

[`to_graphml()`](../reference/to_graphml.qmd) writes a graph, and
[`from_graphml()`](../reference/from_graphml.qmd) reads one back:

```{python}
ec.to_graphml(lab, "lab.graphml")
print(Path("lab.graphml").read_text()[:1100])
```

Each node is written with its label as its GraphML `id`, so the files are readable and other tools
show the right names. The attributes keep their types: booleans become `boolean`, integers `long`,
other numbers `double`, and strings `string`. Lists, dictionaries, and attributes whose values have
mixed types are stored as JSON strings and marked so that `from_graphml()` decodes them again. The
graph's name, its direction, and the edge weights are kept as well. Reading the file back gives
the same graph:

```{python}
lab2 = ec.from_graphml("lab.graphml")
lab2.get_graph_name(), lab2.is_weighted(), lab2.get_node_df().equals(lab.get_node_df())
```

When reading a file written by another program, `from_graphml()` takes the direction from the
file's `edgedefault` setting and treats the graph as weighted when the edges have a `weight` key.
Both can be overridden with `directed=` and `weighted=`. A node key named `label`, as Gephi and
Cytoscape write, supplies the node labels, and otherwise the GraphML `id` does. Only the first graph
in a file is read.

## GEXF

GEXF is the native format of [Gephi](https://gephi.org), the desktop application for exploring and
drawing large networks. Besides the attributes, it holds Gephi's *visualization data*: the position,
color, and size of each node. [`to_gexf()`](../reference/to_gexf.qmd) writes a node's `pos`
attribute, set by any of the `layout_*()` methods, as its position, a hex `color` attribute as its
color, and a numeric `size` attribute as its size. A graph prepared in EdgeCase therefore opens in
Gephi already laid out and colored. For the karate club, with its factions as colors, PageRank as
the node size, and a ForceAtlas2 layout:

```{python}
karate = ec.karate_club()
karate.layout_forceatlas2(linlog=True, seed=1)
karate.colorize_node_attrs("faction", palette="Set2")
karate.pagerank()
karate.rescale_node_attrs("pagerank", range=[10, 40])

ec.to_gexf(karate, "karate.gexf", description="Zachary's karate club", keywords=["social"])
```

The two `colorize_node_attrs()` and `rescale_node_attrs()` methods are described in
[Aesthetics](24-aesthetics.qmd#visual-attributes-for-the-interactive-views). `description=` and
`keywords=` fill in the file's metadata, which Gephi shows in its project overview. The work can
also go the other way. [`from_gexf()`](../reference/from_gexf.qmd) reads Gephi's positions back into
a `pos` attribute, and its colors and sizes into `color` and `size`, so a layout made by hand in
Gephi can be drawn by `plot()`:

```{python}
from_gephi = ec.from_gexf("karate.gexf")
from_gephi.plot(layout="pos", color_by="faction", show_labels=False, node_size=7)
```

`return_meta=True` also returns the file's metadata, such as its creator and description, as a
dictionary. GEXF versions 1.1, 1.2, and 1.3 are read, and the time information of dynamic graphs is
ignored. Since Gephi doesn't require node labels to be unique, a file whose labels repeat is read
with the GEXF node IDs as labels, and the original labels are kept in a `name` attribute.

## GML

GML, the Graph Modelling Language, is a plain-text format of nested blocks. Many of the classic
network science datasets, such as the collections of Mark Newman and of the Pajek project, are
distributed as GML files. A file written by hand or by an older tool might look like this, with a
nested `graphics` block holding drawing information and the edge weights given as `value`:

```{python}
gml_text = """
graph [
  directed 0
  node [ id 0 label "Myriel" graphics [ x 12.5 y -3.0 fill "#ff7f0e" ] ]
  node [ id 1 label "Napoleon" ]
  node [ id 2 label "Mlle Baptistine" ]
  edge [ source 1 target 0 value 1 ]
  edge [ source 2 target 0 value 8 ]
]
"""
Path("miserables.gml").write_text(gml_text)

novel = ec.from_gml("miserables.gml")
novel.get_node_df()
```

[`from_gml()`](../reference/from_gml.qmd) labels each node with its `label` key, and turns every
other key into an attribute: numbers stay numbers, a key repeated within a block becomes a list,
and a nested block such as `graphics` becomes a dictionary, which Polars shows as a struct column.
The GML `id` values only connect the edges to the nodes; EdgeCase assigns its own IDs. Since no edge
has a `weight` key, the `value` keys were taken as the weights:

```{python}
novel.get_edge_df()
```

[`to_gml()`](../reference/to_gml.qmd) writes all the attributes too. GML has no boolean type, so
`True` and `False` are written as 1 and 0 and come back as integers, and an empty list has no GML
representation and comes back as a missing value. A graph with parallel edges is marked as a
multigraph, which NetworkX requires before it reads one.

## Pajek and LEDA

[Pajek](http://mrvar.fdv.uni-lj.si/pajek/) is a program for the analysis of large networks, and its
`.net` format is a simple, line-based text format that many older social network datasets use.
Vertices are numbered and listed with their labels, followed by the edges, under `*Edges` for an
undirected graph or `*Arcs` for a directed one:

```{python}
ec.to_pajek(lab, "lab.net")
print(Path("lab.net").read_text())
```

[`to_pajek()`](../reference/to_pajek.qmd) writes each attribute as a `key value` pair after its
vertex or edge, and a `pos` attribute as the vertex coordinates. Pajek values are single words or
numbers, so attributes holding lists or dictionaries are left out with a warning, and booleans
become 1 and 0. [`from_pajek()`](../reference/from_pajek.qmd) reads all of this back, and two
features of Pajek files in particular. In a two-mode network, declared as `*Vertices n n1`, the
first `n1` vertices get a `part` attribute of 0 and the rest a `part` of 1, which suits
[`layout_bipartite()`](../reference/Graph.layout_bipartite.qmd). And a relation named in a section
header, as in `*Arcs :2 "advice"`, becomes the `rel` of the edges in that section, so a file with
several relations is read into one graph whose edges can be told apart.

The native graph format of the LEDA C++ library is still used by graph algorithm benchmarks. It
stores node labels and one value per edge. [`to_leda()`](../reference/to_leda.qmd) writes the edge
weights as that value, and like several of the text writers, it returns the text when no path is
given:

```{python}
print(ec.to_leda(lab))
```

The `-2` on the fourth line marks the graph as undirected.
[`from_leda()`](../reference/from_leda.qmd) reads numeric edge values as weights, and any other edge
values into a `label` attribute.

## Edge lists

The simplest way to store a network is a list of its edges, one per line. Interaction databases
such as BioGRID, STRING, and IntAct export their data this way, often with extra columns of
scores and evidence, and most spreadsheets and scripts can produce such a file.

[`from_tsv_edge_list()`](../reference/from_tsv_edge_list.qmd) reads a delimited file, with the
source, target, and an optional weight in the columns given by `source_col=`, `target_col=`, and
`weight_col=`. These are column positions by default, counting from 0, and can be column names
when the file has a header. A protein network downloaded from STRING, for example, is separated by
spaces, has a header, and gives a confidence score for each interaction:

```{python}
string_text = """protein1 protein2 combined_score
9606.TP53 9606.MDM2 999
9606.TP53 9606.CDKN1A 987
9606.MDM2 9606.MDM4 962
9606.CDKN1A 9606.CDK2 941
9606.TP53 9606.ATM 903
"""
Path("string.txt").write_text(string_text)

p53 = ec.from_tsv_edge_list(
    "string.txt",
    delimiter=" ",
    has_header=True,
    source_col="protein1",
    target_col="protein2",
    weight_col="combined_score",
)
p53.get_edge_df()
```

Each protein becomes a node labelled with its STRING identifier, in order of first appearance, and
the scores become weights, which makes the graph weighted. Lines starting with `comment=` (`#` by
default) are skipped, `skip_rows=` skips a preamble, and `directed=True` reads the edges as
directed. Lines with too few columns are skipped rather than raising an error, which copes with
the stray blank or truncated lines that large downloads sometimes have, and an edge whose weight
isn't a number is added without a weight.

[`to_tsv_edge_list()`](../reference/to_tsv_edge_list.qmd) writes the labels of each edge's
endpoints and, for a weighted graph, its weight, with a header line by default. An edge list holds
edges and nothing else, so isolated nodes and attributes are lost:

```{python}
ec.to_tsv_edge_list(lab, "lab.tsv")
print(Path("lab.tsv").read_text())
```

Dev, who has no edges, is not in the file. When isolated nodes or attributes matter, use a richer
format, or write the node table as a second file as described in
[Tables of nodes and edges](#tables-of-nodes-and-edges) below.

### Simple Interaction Format

SIF is the text format of [Cytoscape](https://cytoscape.org), the platform for visualizing
biological networks. Each line holds a node, an interaction type, and one or more nodes it
interacts with, and a node on a line by itself is an isolated node. The interaction type is kept
in each edge's `rel`, so [`to_sif()`](../reference/to_sif.qmd) and
[`from_sif()`](../reference/from_sif.qmd) preserve the kinds of relationship:

```{python}
ec.to_sif(lab, "lab.sif")
print(Path("lab.sif").read_text())
```

Edges without a `rel` are written with the `interaction_type=` of the call, `"interacts_with"` by
default. SIF has no place for weights or attributes. It also doesn't record whether a network is
directed, so `from_sif()` reads an undirected graph unless `directed=True` is passed.

### Matrix Market

The Matrix Market format stores a sparse matrix as a list of its nonzero entries, and is the format
of the SuiteSparse Matrix Collection and of several network repositories. Read as a graph, each
entry is an edge, weighted by its value. EdgeCase stores its own datasets in this format (see
[Datasets](06-datasets.qmd)). The header line says whether the matrix is `symmetric`, an undirected
graph, or `general`, a directed one, and whether its entries are `real` or `integer` values or only
a `pattern` of positions, which gives an unweighted graph:

```{python}
mtx_text = """%%MatrixMarket matrix coordinate real symmetric
% a small weighted network
4 4 4
2 1 1.5
3 2 2.0
4 3 0.5
4 1 3.0
"""
Path("ring.mtx").write_text(mtx_text)

ring = ec.from_matrix_market("ring.mtx")
ring.is_directed(), ring.get_node_df()["label"].to_list(), ring.get_edge_df()["weight"].to_list()
```

[`from_matrix_market()`](../reference/from_matrix_market.qmd) detects both properties from the
header, and `directed=` and `weighted=` override them. Matrix Market numbers its rows and columns
from 1, and the nodes are labelled from `"0"`, so row 1 becomes the node labelled `"0"`, the
convention of the network repositories whose datasets EdgeCase includes. The format holds no node
labels or attributes. There is no writer, since the formats above suit exchanging graphs better.

## Adjacency lists

An adjacency list gives each node on a line of its own, followed by its neighbors. It is the
compact text format of NetworkX's `write_adjlist()`, and a convenient one for small graphs typed by
hand. [`from_adjlist()`](../reference/from_adjlist.qmd) reads a file, a list of lines, or the text
itself, when the string has at least one line break:

```{python}
road = ec.from_adjlist(
    """
    # each town and the towns it has a road to
    Avon Bray Crewe
    Bray Dover
    Crewe Dover Ely
    Fenwick
    """
)
road.count_nodes(), road.count_edges(), road.get_node_df()["label"].to_list()
```

Every name becomes a node: first the towns that start a line, in order, then those that appear only
as neighbors, such as Ely. Fenwick has a line of its own and no neighbors, so it is kept as an
isolated node. Names are separated by whitespace, or by `delimiter=`, and a pair of nodes listed
twice gives a single edge unless `parallel_edges=True`.
[`to_adjlist()`](../reference/to_adjlist.qmd) writes the same layout, listing each undirected edge
once. It keeps only the structure, and since the names are separated by spaces, it raises an error
for labels that contain whitespace, the delimiter, or `#`.

The *multiline* variant keeps the edge data as well. Each node's line gives its number of
neighbors, and each neighbor follows on a line of its own, with the edge's data as a Python
dictionary:

```{python}
print(ec.to_multiline_adjlist(lab))
```

[`from_multiline_adjlist()`](../reference/from_multiline_adjlist.qmd) reads the weights and
attributes back. Neither variant holds node attributes.

## JSON formats

JSON is the natural format for graphs that travel to and from web applications and JavaScript
libraries. EdgeCase reads and writes four JSON layouts. Each `to_*()` function returns the data as
a Python dictionary, ready for `json.dumps()` or a web framework, and also writes it to a file when
a path is given. Each `from_*()` function accepts a dictionary, a JSON string, or a path.

### Node-link data

The *node-link* layout, with a list of nodes and a list of edges, is the one that
[D3.js](https://d3js.org) force layouts use, and NetworkX's `node_link_data()` writes.
[`to_node_link()`](../reference/to_node_link.qmd) gives each node its label as its `id`, along
with its attributes, and each edge its endpoints, its weight, and its attributes:

```{python}
import json

data = ec.to_node_link(lab)
print(json.dumps(data, indent=2)[:600])
```

The `directed` and `multigraph` fields describe the graph, and `graph` holds its name.
[`from_node_link()`](../reference/from_node_link.qmd) reads this layout, and also the older one
with `links` instead of `edges`, which D3 examples and earlier versions of NetworkX use. The
round trip keeps everything:

```{python}
ec.from_node_link(data).get_edge_df().equals(lab.get_edge_df())
```

`to_node_link(edges="links")` writes the older layout for tools that expect it.

### Cytoscape.js

[Cytoscape.js](https://js.cytoscape.org) is a JavaScript library for interactive network
visualization, used in many biological web applications.
[`to_cytoscape()`](../reference/to_cytoscape.qmd) writes the `elements` it expects, which the
Cytoscape desktop application can open as a `.cyjs` file as well:

```{python}
elements = ec.to_cytoscape(lab)
elements["elements"]["nodes"][0], elements["elements"]["edges"][0]
```

Each element has its fields in a `data` dictionary, and each edge gets an `id` of its own. A node's
`pos` attribute becomes its `position`, with the y axis flipped, since it points down on screen.
[`from_cytoscape()`](../reference/from_cytoscape.qmd) reads the elements back, either as separate
`nodes` and `edges` lists or as one flat list, and turns positions into a `pos` attribute, so a
layout arranged in a Cytoscape application can be drawn with `plot(layout="pos")`.

### Adjacency and tree data

Two more layouts come from NetworkX. The *adjacency* layout of
[`to_adjacency_data()`](../reference/to_adjacency_data.qmd) lists each node's edges under the node,
which is convenient for code that walks the graph node by node, and
[`from_adjacency_data()`](../reference/from_adjacency_data.qmd) reads it.

The *tree* layout nests each node's children inside the node, the shape of a D3.js hierarchy, used
by tree maps, sunbursts, and collapsible trees.
[`from_tree_data()`](../reference/from_tree_data.qmd) builds a tree from the nested data, with edges
from each parent to its children:

```{python}
taxonomy = {
    "id": "Animals",
    "children": [
        {"id": "Mammals", "species": 6400, "children": [{"id": "Whales"}, {"id": "Bats"}]},
        {"id": "Birds", "species": 11000},
    ],
}
tree = ec.from_tree_data(taxonomy)
tree.get_node_df()
```

The fields other than the ID and the children become node attributes, and the nodes are added in
depth-first order. `ident=` and `children=` name the two special fields when the data uses others,
such as `name` and `kids`. [`to_tree_data()`](../reference/to_tree_data.qmd) nests a tree again,
starting from a given root:

```{python}
ec.to_tree_data(tree, root="Animals")
```

The graph must be a tree, and a directed one must have its edges pointing away from the root.

### Dictionaries

[`from_dict_of_dicts()`](../reference/from_dict_of_dicts.qmd) and
[`from_dict_of_lists()`](../reference/from_dict_of_lists.qmd) build graphs from nested Python
dictionaries, which is how graphs are often kept in plain Python code or loaded from JSON
configuration files. In a dict of dicts, each node maps to its neighbors, and each neighbor to the
data of the edge. In a dict of lists, each node maps to a list of its neighbors:

```{python}
flights = ec.from_dict_of_dicts(
    {
        "LHR": {"JFK": {"weight": 5540}, "CDG": {"weight": 344}},
        "CDG": {"JFK": {"weight": 5837}},
    },
    directed=True,
)
flights.is_weighted(), flights.get_edge_df()["weight"].to_list()
```

A numeric `weight` in the edge data sets the edge weights and makes the graph weighted, and any
other fields become edge attributes. [`to_dict_of_dicts()`](../reference/to_dict_of_dicts.qmd) and
[`to_dict_of_lists()`](../reference/to_dict_of_lists.qmd) convert a graph the other way, keyed by
node labels:

```{python}
ec.to_dict_of_lists(lab)
```

These dictionaries match the ones NetworkX produces and accepts, which is described further in
[Other libraries](28-other-libraries.qmd).

## graph6 and sparse6

graph6 and sparse6 are the compact formats of [nauty](https://pallini.di.uniroma1.it), the program
for graph isomorphism, and of the [House of Graphs](https://houseofgraphs.org), a database of
interesting graphs. Each graph is a single line of printable characters. graph6 encodes the upper
triangle of the adjacency matrix, which suits dense graphs, and sparse6 encodes the list of edges,
which suits sparse ones. The Petersen graph, for example:

```{python}
petersen = ec.Graph().add_named_graph("petersen")
ec.to_graph6(petersen), ec.to_sparse6(petersen)
```

The formats store nothing but the structure of an undirected graph: the order of the nodes is kept,
but labels, weights, and attributes aren't, and writing a directed graph raises an error.
[`from_graph6()`](../reference/from_graph6.qmd) and
[`from_sparse6()`](../reference/from_sparse6.qmd) label the nodes `"1"` to `"n"`. A file or string
with several lines, such as a download from the House of Graphs or the output of nauty's `geng`
generator, gives a list of graphs. All three graphs on three nodes with at least one edge, read at
once:

```{python}
small = ec.from_graph6("B_\nBg\nBw\n")
[(graph.count_nodes(), graph.count_edges()) for graph in small]
```

Collections in this form make good test cases: they enumerate every graph of a given size, so an
algorithm can be checked against all of them in a loop.

## DOT

DOT is the graph language of [Graphviz](https://graphviz.org), and many tools write it, including
compilers, documentation generators, build systems, and infrastructure tools such as Terraform.
[`from_dot()`](../reference/from_dot.qmd) reads the full language, including chains of edges,
subgraphs, and default attributes for the nodes and edges that follow them:

```{python}
pipeline = ec.from_dot(
    """
    digraph build {
        node [shape=box];
        fetch -> {compile lint} -> package [color=gray];
        package -> deploy;
        lint [label="Static checks"];
    }
    """
)
pipeline.get_graph_name(), pipeline.count_nodes(), pipeline.count_edges()
```

The chain from `fetch` through `{compile lint}` to `package` makes four edges, one for each path
through the braces, and each gets the `color` attribute given at the end of the chain. The `node
[shape=box]` default gives every node a `shape` attribute:

```{python}
pipeline.get_edge_df()
```

Each node's DOT name becomes its label. A DOT `label` attribute, such as the "Static checks" of
`lint`, is display text for Graphviz, and it is kept as an attribute that `to_dot()` writes back.
DOT has only strings, so every attribute is read as a string, except that a numeric edge `weight`
becomes the edge weight. Graph attributes, such as `rankdir=LR`, and the grouping of nodes into
subgraphs are read but not kept. A file with several graphs gives a list of graphs.

[`to_dot()`](../reference/to_dot.qmd) writes a graph as DOT, ready to be drawn by Graphviz with a
command such as `dot -Tsvg build.dot -o build.svg`:

```{python}
print(ec.to_dot(pipeline))
```

Values are quoted only where DOT requires it. Since Graphviz interprets attributes such as
`shape`, `color`, `label`, and `style`, setting them on a graph in EdgeCase is a way to control a
Graphviz drawing, for example with a `color` attribute from `colorize_node_attrs()`.

## LaTeX and TikZ

[`to_latex()`](../reference/to_latex.qmd) writes LaTeX code that draws a graph with
[TikZ](https://tikz.dev), for figures in papers and theses that match the fonts and style of the
document. The nodes are placed at the positions in their `pos` attribute, so a `layout_*()` method
comes first:

```{python}
lab.layout_kamada_kawai()
print(
    ec.to_latex(
        lab,
        tikz_options="[scale=2]",
        default_node_options="[circle, draw]",
        caption="Collaborations in the lab.",
        latex_label="fig:lab",
    )
)
```

By default the result is a complete document that compiles as it is with `pdflatex`, and
`as_document=False` gives only the `figure` environment, for pasting into an existing document.
The layout positions are about 1 unit across, and TikZ units are centimeters, so `scale=` is
usually needed to give the drawing a reasonable size. The look of the drawing is controlled with
TikZ options: `default_node_options=` and `default_edge_options=` apply to all nodes and edges, and
`node_options=`, `node_label=`, `edge_options=`, and `edge_label=` set them for individual nodes and
edges, either from an attribute or from a dictionary:

```{python}
#| eval: false
ec.to_latex(
    lab,
    tikz_options="[scale=2]",
    default_node_options="[circle, draw, fill=white]",
    node_options={"Ada": "fill=orange!30"},
    edge_label={("Ada", "Bo"): "5 papers"},
    edge_label_options={("Ada", "Bo"): "[above, sloped]"},
    filepath="lab-figure.tex",
)
```

A list of graphs gives a figure with one subfigure per graph, arranged in `n_rows=` rows, with
`sub_captions=` for their captions, which suits a before-and-after comparison.
[`to_latex_raw()`](../reference/to_latex_raw.qmd) gives the bare `tikzpicture` environment, for
documents that place it themselves. The output matches that of NetworkX's functions of the same
names.

## Cypher

[`from_cypher()`](../reference/from_cypher.qmd) reads the `CREATE` statements of the Cypher query
language, and [`to_cypher()`](../reference/to_cypher.qmd) writes a graph as one, which moves graphs
to and from graph databases such as Neo4j and Memgraph. Both are described in
[Cypher queries](10-cypher.qmd#exchanging-graphs-with-cypher-databases).

## Tables of nodes and edges

Much network data lives in tables rather than in graph formats: CSV files, Parquet files,
spreadsheets, and databases. Polars reads and writes all of these, so the general route is to go
through the node and edge tables. [`get_node_df()`](../reference/Graph.get_node_df.qmd) and
[`get_edge_df()`](../reference/Graph.get_edge_df.qmd) give the tables, which Polars can write in any
of its formats. Parquet is a good choice, since it is compact and fast, and keeps the column types,
including lists and structs:

```{python}
karate.get_node_df().write_parquet("karate-nodes.parquet")
karate.get_edge_df().write_parquet("karate-edges.parquet")
```

The `Graph` constructor then builds the graph from the tables again (see
[Building graphs](04-building-graphs.qmd#building-a-graph-from-dataframes)). It expects the edge
endpoints in columns named `from` and `to`, so the `source` and `target` columns need renaming, and
the `degree` column, which EdgeCase computes rather than stores, is best dropped:

```{python}
nodes = pl.read_parquet("karate-nodes.parquet").drop("degree")
edges = pl.read_parquet("karate-edges.parquet").rename({"source": "from", "target": "to"})

restored = ec.Graph(nodes_df=nodes, edges_df=edges)
same_nodes = restored.get_node_df().equals(karate.get_node_df())
same_edges = restored.get_edge_df().equals(karate.get_edge_df())
same_nodes, same_edges
```

The restored graph is identical to the original, with every attribute, including the PageRank
scores, the colors, and the layout positions. This works because the node table has both an `id`
and a `label` column: the labels become the node labels, and the `from` and `to` values are looked
up in the `id` column, so the edges connect the right nodes. For a weighted graph, pass
`weighted=True` to the constructor so that the `weight` column sets the weights, and `directed=True`
for a directed one.

The same route reads tables that were never written by EdgeCase. An edge table from a database or a
CSV file needs only its endpoint columns renamed to `from` and `to`, and a node table, if there is
one, its identifier column to `id`; then the edge endpoints are matched against that column.

## Choosing a format

The choice of format usually follows from where the graph is going or where it came from. When the
choice is open:

| Need | Format |
|---|---|
| Keep everything, for any other tool | GraphML |
| Lay out or explore the graph in Gephi | GEXF |
| Analyze it in Cytoscape | GraphML, Cytoscape.js JSON, or SIF |
| Draw it with D3.js or another web library | node-link JSON |
| Draw it with Graphviz | DOT |
| Put a figure in a LaTeX document | `to_latex()` |
| Store it compactly, with all attributes and types | Parquet node and edge tables |
| Share the edges with any program or spreadsheet | a TSV edge list |
| Catalog many small unlabelled graphs | graph6 or sparse6 |
| Load it into a graph database | Cypher |

Whatever the format, a quick round trip, writing the graph and reading it back, followed by a
comparison of `get_node_df()` and `get_edge_df()` with the originals, shows exactly what a format
keeps for a particular graph.
